title: Right to Remain Silent
before: That protection covers your testimony in court. It does not cover things you say to a social worker or anyone else outside of court.
after: The law talks only about what you say as a witness in court. It does not say that what you tell a social worker is protected.

title: Right to Remain Silent
before: If the social worker or county counsel asks you questions outside of court, you have the right to say "I want to talk to my attorney first."
after: If a social worker or the county's lawyer asks you questions outside of court, you can say "I want to talk to my lawyer first." Ask your lawyer how to handle these talks.

title: Right to Participate in Case Planning
before: WIC §16501.1 – Case plan must be developed with parent participation.
after: WIC §16501.1(g)(12): Parents take part in making the case plan whenever possible, and get a chance to read and sign it.

title: Right to Participate in Case Planning
before: Parents have the right to argue for services and placements at disposition.
after: Parents have the right to argue for services and placements at disposition (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.534(g), right to present evidence at hearings).

title: Right to Be Heard in Court
before: If you are a relative caregiver, foster parent, or other important person in the child's life, you can provide input to the court through a Caregiver Information Form
after: If the child lives with you (as a relative caregiver, foster parent, or close family friend), you can tell the judge about the child with the Caregiver Information Form (JV-290) or a letter. If you are a relative but the child does not live with you, use the Relative Information form (JV-285)

title: Right to Be Heard in Court
before: or by speaking at hearings.
after: . You can also ask the judge to let you speak at the hearing.

title: Right to Be Heard in Court
before: You can tell the judge how the child is doing. Use the Caregiver Information Form or speak at a hearing.
after: If the child lives with you, you can tell the judge how the child is doing. Use the Caregiver Information Form (JV-290) or a letter, or ask the judge to let you speak.

title: Right to Your Own Attorney
before: Your attorney should come visit you or talk to you on the phone before hearings.
after: Your lawyer is expected to meet with you regularly and stay in touch with you.

title: Right to Privacy
before: Your belongings should travel with you if you change placements — no one should throw away your stuff.
after: If your placement changes, ask your social worker to make sure all your things move with you.

title: Right to Participate in Your Case Plan
before: Ask your social worker to go over the plan with you and to give you a copy.
after: Ask your social worker to go over the plan with you. If you are 10 or older you have the right to look at it. If you are 12 or older and in a permanent placement, you have the right to a copy.

title: Communicate Regularly with the Team
before: Form JV-290 is due 5 days before the hearing (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.534(k)).
after: Form JV-290 is due 5 calendar days before the hearing if you hand it in at court, or 7 calendar days before if you mail it (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.534(k)(4)).

title: Right to Prepare for Adulthood
before: If you are 14 or older, you have the right to services to help you prepare for independent living.
after: If you are 14 or older, your case plan must list the programs and services that will help you get ready for adult life. At 16, you also get your own plan for living on your own (called a TILP).

title: Right to Prepare for Adulthood
before: This includes life skills, education planning, and help with jobs and housing.
after: Starting at 16, the Independent Living Program (ILP) can help with daily living skills, money, school, jobs, and housing.

title: Right to Prepare for Adulthood
before: If you are 14 or older, you get help getting ready for adult life, like school, jobs, and housing.
after: At 14, your case plan must list help to get you ready for adult life. At 16, you can join the Independent Living Program for help with school, jobs, and housing.

title: Right to Prepare for Adulthood
before: Ask about Independent Living Program (ILP) services. You can learn cooking, budgeting, and other life skills.
after: Ask about Independent Living Program (ILP) services. ILP starts at 16. Ask your social worker if your county offers anything for younger teens.

title: Right to Prepare for Adulthood
note: field now reads WIC §16501.1(g)(16); WIC §16001.9(a). The bare §16501 cite is gone. It cites (a), not (a)(29) as the fix has it.

title: Right to Notice of Hearings
before: The court must give you written notice that includes the date, time, and location of the hearing, and what will be discussed.
after: You must be told the date, time, and place of each hearing. For the very first hearing, the social worker tells you, and it can be out loud instead of on paper. After that, notice comes in writing and says what the hearing is about.

title: Right to Notice of Hearings
before: You must be told in writing when and where each hearing is.
after: You must be told when and where each hearing is. Notice of the first hearing can be out loud, and later notices come in writing.
note: fix joined into two sentences to keep simple_text short

title: Right to Reasonable Efforts
before: The agency must make reasonable efforts to prevent removal and to reunify families.
after: The county must make reasonable efforts to keep a child at home. If a child is removed, the county must usually give the parents services to help the family reunify. In some serious cases the judge can decide the county does not have to offer those services.
note: role is both, so the fix's 'your child' was worded as 'a child' and 'the parents'; no fact changed

title: Right to Reasonable Efforts
before: At each hearing, the judge checks whether the agency provided adequate services.
after: When the judge removes a child and at each review hearing, the judge must decide whether the county made reasonable efforts and gave reasonable services.

title: Right to Reasonable Efforts
before: The county has to really try to keep your family together. The judge checks on this at each hearing.
after: The county usually has to really try to keep your family together, and the judge checks on this at review hearings. In some serious cases the judge can say the county does not have to offer services.
note: fix joined into two sentences to keep simple_text short

title: Right to Be Treated Fairly
before: You cannot be discriminated against because of your race, gender, sexual orientation, religion, disability, or any other reason.
after: You cannot be treated unfairly or harassed because of your race, ethnic group, where your family is from, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, or HIV status.

title: Right to Be Treated Fairly
before: Talk to your attorney or call the Ombudsman.
note: field now says Ombudsperson, not Ombudsman. The phone number from the fix is not in this sentence.

title: Speak Up When Something Is Wrong
before: it is your responsibility to tell someone.
after: you have the right to tell someone. Please tell an adult you trust so they can help.

title: Right to Go to School
before: You can usually stay at your same school even if you move to a new home, when you and the adult who makes your school decisions agree it is best for you.
note: field already has the corrected wording

title: Right to Relevant Information
after: WIC §16010(c) (the agency must give the caregiver the health and education summary); see also WIC §16010.4

title: Right to Suggest Relative Placement
before: Relatives must be assessed by the agency, but they have priority over non-relative foster homes.
after: Relatives must be checked by the agency. They are looked at first, before foster homes with people the child does not know. Being first in line does not mean the child will always be placed with them.

title: Right to Suggest Relative Placement
before: Noncustodial parent has right to custody unless detrimental to child.
after: Noncustodial parent has right to custody unless detrimental to child (WIC §361.2).

title: Support the Case Plan

title: Maintain Sobriety (If Applicable)
before: The court will likely require regular drug testing.
after: The judge may order drug testing as part of your case plan.

title: Maintain Sobriety (If Applicable)
before: Missing a test is usually treated the same as a failed test.
after: A missed test may be counted as a failed test. Ask your lawyer how your court treats a missed test.

title: Maintain Sobriety (If Applicable)
before: A missed test usually counts as a failed one.
after: A missed test may count as a failed one, so ask your lawyer how your court treats it.

title: Maintain Sobriety (If Applicable)
before: If you relapse, be honest with your attorney and treatment provider — a relapse does not automatically mean your case is over, but hiding it will make things worse.
after: If you relapse, tell your lawyer and your treatment provider right away and get back into treatment. Hiding it will make things worse.

title: Right to Request De Facto Parent Status
before: This gives you the right to be at hearings, to have a lawyer, and to give the judge evidence.
after: This lets you be at hearings, bring a lawyer you hire, and give the judge evidence. The judge may give you a free lawyer but does not have to.

title: Extended Foster Care (After 18)
before: You do not have to leave foster care at 18. You can stay until 21 and get help with housing, school, and work.
after: You do not have to leave foster care at 18. You can stay until 21 if you are in school, working, in a job program, or have a health condition that stops you.

title: Extended Foster Care (After 18)
before: You need to meet at least one condition: working, in school, in a job training program, or have a medical condition that prevents these.
after: You need to meet at least one condition: in school, in a job program, working at least 80 hours a month, or having a medical condition that stops you from doing these.

title: Be Honest with the Court
before: If the social worker asks you something and you are not sure how to answer, say "I want to talk to my attorney before answering."
after: If you are not sure how to answer the social worker, ask your lawyer what to do.

title: Relative Placement Preference
before: Even if the child is already placed elsewhere, you can still request to be considered.
after: You can still ask if the child is already placed somewhere else. After the disposition hearing, the law says relatives must be looked at first again when the child needs a new placement.

title: Relative Placement Preference
before: The faster you complete the approval, the better chance the child has of being placed with you.
after: Ask about emergency placement. The child may be able to move in after a safety check, before full approval. You then have 5 business days to apply.

before: Include all costs you can think of, including therapy and special needs.
after: Tell the worker about all of the child's needs, like therapy or special care. The payment is based on those needs and cannot be more than the foster care rate.

before: They can help with problems at your placement, school issues, or if your rights are not being respected.
